steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction to a position paper comparing today's LLM era in NLP with the earlier statistical machine translation era, opening with an anecdote and previewing the lessons the paper draws for researchers worried about scale.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Opening scene: a keynote that shakes the field
- Reveal: it happened in 2005, the SMT era
- MT research survived and flourished
- Today's scale crisis and what researchers should do
- Lessons (one per section)
- Conclusion: do research

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - results slide (Figure 1): Google improved SMT just by expanding training corpus of a phrase-based language model
- MT survived
  - first LLM era caused anxiety among MT researchers
  - MT research kept flourishing in academia, industry, government
  - deep learning era: MT a locus of innovations that altered NLP and all of ML
- Current era
  - massive proprietary models a de facto baseline for many tasks
  - expense of SOTA research -> questions about role of smaller, publicly funded groups in AI; "scale crisis"
  - researchers without LLM access fret publicly; one paper suggests pivots to sidestep scale; another sketches areas "not within the purview of LLMs."
  - but what about problems within the purview of LLMs? look to first era: durable lessons, evergreen problems
- Lessons
  - Scale is supreme (Section 2): Bitter Lesson, general purpose methods exploiting scale beat informed priors where data plentiful; use hardware improvements for scale at affordable budgets (2.1); remember small-scale problems (2.2)
  - Evaluation is a bottleneck (Section 3): generic methods need metrics to optimize; better models -> subtle/edge-case errors harder to detect; automated metrics flawed at scale; improve metrics (3.1)
  - There is no gold standard (Section 4): human feedback tempting; naive preference solicitation -> poor feedback, superficial properties; counterpoint to collecting massive low-quality data; ground measurement in concrete downstream tasks (4.1)

- Conclusion: Do research (Section 6)

  - renew commitment to foundational science even where scale dominates

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Picture this scene: A renowned NLP researcher from a hot seven-year-old startup gets onstage to give a keynote. The speaker describes an ambitious new system to the packed room and builds up to the results slide, which is a bar chart where the x -axis shows the number of training words and the y -axis shows system accuracy. As each data point is revealed, the performance keeps going up, ending with a system trained on well over a trillion words using over a thousand processor cores. It beats the state of the art by a margin that people thought was impossible.

The attendees are visibly shaken as they realize, within a minute, that years of research were just made completely inconsequential. Established academics panic, because they expect their already-submitted grant applications to be rejected. PhD students despair, thinking about how their unfinished dissertations are now irrelevant. Many think about leaving for industry or changing fields. They will talk about little else this week.

Does this sound like a scene that might have happened in the past year? Actually, it happened 19 years ago, in 2005, and it started the first era of Large Language Models (LLMs), which was the Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) era. The speaker was Franz Och, who had co-invented key methods in SMT. He had not published new work since he joined Google in 2004, and instead he revealed it in an invited talk before the launch of a new Google Translate. The provocative results slide from that talk (Figure 1) shows that Google improved its SMT system just by making the training corpus of a phrase-based language model bigger.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Picture this scene: A renowned NLP researcher from a hot seven-year-old startup gets onstage to give a keynote. The speaker describes an ambitious new system to the packed room and builds up to the results slide, which is a bar chart where the x -axis shows the number of training words and the y -axis shows system accuracy. As each data point is revealed, the performance keeps going up, ending with a system trained on well over a trillion words using over a thousand processor cores. It beats the state of the art by a margin that people thought was impossible.

The attendees are visibly shaken as they realize, within a minute, that years of research were just made completely inconsequential. Established academics panic, because they expect their already-submitted grant applications to be rejected. PhD students despair, thinking about how their unfinished dissertations are now irrelevant. Many think about leaving for industry or changing fields. They will talk about little else this week.

Does this sound like a scene that might have happened in the past year? Actually, it happened 19 years ago, in 2005, and it started the first era of Large Language Models (LLMs), which was the Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) era. The speaker was Franz Och, who had co-invented key methods in SMT. He had not published new work since he joined Google in 2004, and instead he revealed it in an invited talk before the launch of a new Google Translate. The provocative results slide from that talk (Figure 1) shows that Google improved its SMT system just by making the training corpus of a phrase-based language model bigger.

The first era of LLMs caused a lot of anxiety among MT researchers about the state of their field at first, but MT research continued to flourish in academia, industry and government. Even in the modern era of deep learning, MT has been a place where innovations happened that fundamentally changed NLP and all of machine learning.

We think this history has lessons for the current era of LLMs, in which massive proprietary models have become a de facto baseline for many tasks. Because state-of-the-art research is so expensive, many people have questioned the role of smaller and publicly funded groups in AI, and we will call this the scale crisis. Researchers who do not have direct access to LLMs have publicly worried about their research directions. One paper suggests pivoting research directions to sidestep scale, and another sketches research areas that are "not within the purview of LLMs." But what should researchers do if the problems they care about are within the purview of LLMs? To answer this, we look at the first era of LLMs. What lessons from that time lasted, and what research problems from then still matter today? We arrive at several lessons that recur:

Scale is supreme (Section 2). We argue that in areas where there is plenty of data, NLP researchers cannot escape the Bitter Lesson, which is that general purpose methods that exploit scale will outperform methods that use informed priors. We recommend that researchers take advantage of hardware improvements since they make scale possible at affordable budgets (Section 2.1), and that they remember small-scale problems (Section 2.2).

Evaluation is a bottleneck (Section 3). The Bitter Lesson favors generic methods, and those need evaluation metrics to optimize over. But when models improve there is an evaluation bottleneck, since it gets harder to detect errors when most of the remaining mistakes are subtle or have to do with edge cases. At scale, automated metrics show their flaws. We recommend that researchers work on improving metrics (Section 3.1).

There is no gold standard (Section 4). If you can afford the annotation costs, it can be tempting to think of human feedback as the ideal solution to the evaluation problem. But history has shown again and again that naïve ways of soliciting human preferences give poor feedback that prioritizes superficial properties of model outputs. This lesson can be a counterpoint to the impulse to collect massive amounts of low-quality data because of the Bitter Lesson. Instead, we recommend grounding performance measurement in concrete downstream tasks (Section 4.1).

Progress is not continuous (Section 5). When neural MT came along it abruptly ended SMT's decade of growth that seemed unbeatable. This change of direction was made possible by new hardware-based paradigms, so we recommend that researchers keep exploring new methods that might scale well on future hardware (Section 5.1).

We conclude with a simple message: Do research (Section 6). We remind the reader that engineering achievements do not make scientific achievements insignificant, and we encourage the NLP community to renew its commitment to foundational scientific research, even in areas where scale is currently a dominant factor.
